check-yourself-currying-and-partial-appl.title: Check yourself: currying and partial application

questions.question: add :: Integer -> Integer -> Integer. What is the type of add 3?
options: Integer -> Integer
Integer
A type error — add needs two arguments at once
Integer -> Integer -> Integer
questions.explanation: add really has type Integer -> (Integer -> Integer). Supplying the first Integer consumes the first arrow and leaves the function that consumes the second one: Integer -> Integer.
optionFeedback: Correct — one arrow has been consumed, leaving a function still waiting for the second Integer.
That would be the type of add 3 4, once both arguments have been supplied — add 3 alone is still a function.
Currying means arguments arrive one at a time; add 3 is a perfectly legal, complete value on its own.
That's add's original, unconsumed type — supplying 3 must remove at least one arrow.

questions.question: Why can a tupled function like addPair :: (Integer, Integer) -> Integer NOT be partially applied the way add can?
options: It takes exactly one argument — the whole pair — so there is no intermediate stage to stop at
Tupled functions are not allowed to have arguments
Tuples cannot contain Integers
addPair is not a function, it's a value
questions.explanation: A tupled function has only one arrow in its type: (Integer, Integer) -> Integer. There is nothing to supply 'partially' — the single argument must be a complete, ready-made pair before the function can do anything.
optionFeedback: Correct — with only one arrow, there is no intermediate function value to stop at partway through.
Tupled functions take arguments freely; the issue is that they take just one argument (the pair), not zero.
Tuples of Integers are completely ordinary — (Integer, Integer) is a perfectly valid type.
addPair is a function (Integer, Integer) -> Integer; the limitation is about its arity, not whether it's a function at all.

check-curried-vs-tupled-forms-and-longer.title: Check: curried vs. tupled forms, and longer chains

questions.question: uncurry :: (a -> b -> c) -> (a, b) -> c. What does uncurry rectangleArea (5, 3) compute, and why?
options: 15 — uncurry adapts the curried rectangleArea into a function taking one pair, then applies it to (5, 3), the same result as rectangleArea 5 3
A type error, because rectangleArea is curried and uncurry only accepts tupled functions
(5, 3), because uncurry returns its second argument unchanged
15, but only because rectangleArea's two arguments happen to be different
questions.explanation: uncurry changes the interface of a curried function so it accepts one pair instead of two separate arguments, without changing what it computes. uncurry rectangleArea (5, 3) does exactly the same arithmetic as rectangleArea 5 3, giving 15.
optionFeedback: Correct — this matches the worked example directly: uncurry rectangleArea (5, 3) is 15.
uncurry is defined precisely to accept a curried function and adapt it to a tupled interface — that is its whole purpose, not a restriction against it.
The pair (5, 3) is consumed to produce the result; uncurry does not pass either argument through unchanged.
The result 15 follows from 5 * 3 regardless of whether the two arguments are equal or different — nothing here depends on that.

questions.question: volume :: Integer -> Integer -> Integer -> Integer. What is the type of volume 2 3?
options: Integer -> Integer — two arguments have been supplied, consuming two arrows, leaving one more to go
Integer — volume 2 3 is already a finished number
Integer -> Integer -> Integer, the same as volume 2
A type error, because volume must receive all three arguments together
questions.explanation: volume 2 :: Integer -> Integer -> Integer, and supplying the next argument consumes one more arrow: volume 2 3 :: Integer -> Integer, still waiting for the height before it becomes a plain Integer at volume 2 3 4.
optionFeedback: Correct — each supplied argument removes exactly one arrow; two arguments supplied leaves exactly one arrow remaining.
That is the type of volume 2 3 4, once all three arguments have arrived — volume 2 3 alone is still a function.
volume 2 already consumed one arrow when 2 was supplied; volume 2 3 must have consumed a second one, so its type cannot be identical to volume 2's.
Currying means each argument may be supplied one at a time — volume 2 3 is a perfectly legal, complete function value on its own.

questions.question: Which best describes when a tupled interface, like rectangleAreaPair :: (Integer, Integer) -> Integer, is the better design choice?
options: When the inputs genuinely belong together as one record-like value, or are naturally rearranged as a unit — not merely to avoid writing a curried function
Whenever performance matters, since a tupled function is always faster than a curried one
Never — a curried interface is strictly better in every situation
Only once a function has more than three arguments
questions.explanation: The lesson states this directly: 'Do not curry merely to avoid a tuple. Use a tuple when the values form one meaningful piece of data; use currying when staged configuration or partial application is useful.' The choice is about the data's shape, not a blanket rule or argument count.
optionFeedback: Correct — this is the lesson's own stated rule: a tuple earns its place when the values belong together as one thing, not as a default.
No claim about relative performance is made anywhere in this lesson; the trade-off discussed is about interface shape and usability, not speed.
The lesson explicitly allows for cases where a tuple is the better choice — 'the inputs belong together as one record-like value' — so currying is not framed as universally superior.
Nothing in this lesson ties the curried-vs-tupled choice to how many arguments a function has; volume itself has three arguments and stays curried.

questions.question: What does (subtract 5) 10 evaluate to, and why is subtract needed instead of (-5)?
options: 5, because subtract 5 x computes x - 5, and (-5) alone would parse as the number negative five, not a section
-5, because (-5) is a right section that subtracts 5 from its argument
5, because (-5) 10 works fine and subtract is just an alternative spelling
15, because subtract adds its two arguments
questions.explanation: (-) is the one operator that does not section on the right, because Haskell's grammar already gives (-5) a meaning: the literal number negative five. subtract 5 sidesteps the ambiguity entirely: subtract 5 10 computes 10 - 5 = 5.
optionFeedback: Correct — subtract 5 10 is 10 - 5 = 5, and (-5) is reserved for the number negative five rather than a section.
(-5) is not a section at all in Haskell — it is parsed as the literal number negative five, so (-5) 10 is a type error, not -5.
(-5) 10 is a type error in GHCi, since (-5) is a number, not a function — subtract exists precisely because of this gap.
subtract x y computes y - x, not x + y — it performs subtraction, matching its name.

questions.question: map (*2) [1,2,3] and filter (>5) [3,7,2,9] both use sections as their first argument. Why does this work?
options: map needs a function a -> b and filter needs a -> Bool; (*2) and (>5) are exactly those shapes once one operand is fixed
Sections are a special case map and filter recognise by name
It only works because the lists contain numbers
(*2) and (>5) are lists, and map/filter distribute over lists of functions
questions.explanation: A section like (*2) is exactly a one-argument function — here, Integer -> Integer — because one operand of * has already been supplied. That is precisely the shape map's first argument (a -> b) requires. Likewise (>5) is a -> Bool, which is exactly what filter's predicate must be.
optionFeedback: Correct — a section is just an ordinary function value once one operand is fixed, and its type happens to match what map or filter expects.
map and filter take any (a -> b) or (a -> Bool) function respectively; a section is not special-cased, it just happens to have the right type.
The element type matters for what the section can be applied to, but the reason a section works as an argument is about its function type, not the list's contents.
(*2) and (>5) are functions, not lists — map and filter apply them to each list element one at a time.

questions.question: raiseTo exponent base = base ^ exponent. square = raiseTo 2. What is the type of square, and what does square 5 compute?
options: Integer -> Integer, and square 5 computes 5 ^ 2 = 25
Integer, and square 5 is a type error because square is already a finished number
Integer -> Integer -> Integer, the same as raiseTo
Integer -> Integer, and square 5 computes 2 ^ 5 = 32
questions.explanation: raiseTo 2 fixes the exponent argument, leaving a function that still needs base: Integer -> Integer. Applying it to 5 computes base ^ exponent with base = 5, exponent = 2, i.e. 5 ^ 2 = 25.
optionFeedback: Correct — raiseTo 2 has consumed the exponent argument, and square 5 substitutes base = 5, giving 5 ^ 2 = 25.
square is a function value (Integer -> Integer), not a finished number — it is legitimate to apply it to 5.
One argument (2, the exponent) has already been supplied, so one arrow has been consumed from raiseTo's type.
The order matters: raiseTo's parameters are exponent then base, so raiseTo 2 fixes the EXPONENT at 2, and square 5 computes base ^ exponent = 5 ^ 2, not 2 ^ 5.

questions.question: cleanWords = words . map toLower. Reading right to left, what happens first when cleanWords is applied to a string?
options: map toLower runs first, lowercasing every character
words runs first, splitting the string into a list of words
Both run at the same time
Neither runs until cleanWords is composed with a third function
questions.explanation: f . g applies g first, then f. In words . map toLower, g is map toLower and f is words, so the whole string is lowercased first, and only then split into words.
optionFeedback: Correct — composition applies the right-hand function first, so map toLower runs before words does.
This reverses the order: words is the left-hand (outer) function, so it runs last, on the already-lowercased string.
Haskell evaluates left-to-right through a single-threaded reduction here — there's no concurrency implied by (.); one call genuinely happens before the other.
cleanWords is a complete, two-stage function on its own — applying it to a string right now runs both stages, no third function needed.

questions.question: Why is filter passedMark [35, 50, 67, 101] well-typed when passedMark = between 50 100?
options: between 50 100 has type Integer -> Bool, exactly the predicate shape filter's first argument needs
filter accepts any function regardless of its type
between 50 100 evaluates to a Bool immediately, and filter treats that Bool as a predicate
passedMark is a list, and filter concatenates lists
questions.explanation: between :: Ord a => a -> a -> a -> Bool. Supplying two arguments (50 and 100) leaves a function of type Integer -> Bool — one value left to test, returning a Bool. That is exactly filter :: (a -> Bool) -> [a] -> [a]'s required first argument.
optionFeedback: Correct — two of between's three arguments are already supplied, leaving exactly an Integer -> Bool predicate.
filter is typed: its first argument must be a -> Bool for the same a as the list's element type, or GHC rejects it.
between 50 100 is still a function (Integer -> Bool), not a Bool value — it has not yet been applied to the value it tests.
passedMark is a function (Integer -> Bool), not a list — filter's second argument is the list [35, 50, 67, 101].
